courts.name: Monte-Carlo Country Club
courts.setting: Terraced clay courts stepping down towards the sea
courts.blurb:
The most famous clay in Monaco isn’t actually in Monaco. It sits just across the border, 21 courts stepping down towards the sea.

It all began with one woman. In 1925, an American admirer decided the old club wasn’t good enough for Suzanne Lenglen, so he built her this. When the terraces opened in 1928, Prince Louis II was on the guest list, and the Riviera had found its new favourite stage. A century later, the Masters brings the whole tennis world here every April. It’s still one of the most beautiful places in the world to play.

courts.name: Hotel Cap-Estel
courts.setting: Private hard court among gardens, with the sea just beyond
courts.blurb:
Here is a quiet one. Cap-Estel sits on its own two-hectare peninsula at Èze-sur-Mer, between Nice and Monaco, with the Mediterranean wrapped around it.

It was built in 1899 by Irish writer Frank Harris, a friend of Oscar Wilde, and it has kept famous secrets ever since. Greta Garbo came for the seclusion, the Rolling Stones followed, and the Beatles are said to have found the idea for ‘Michelle’ here.

Today the private tennis court sits among gardens, fountains and pools, with the sea just beyond. A match here feels like the Riviera with its voice lowered.

courts.name: Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc
courts.setting: Five clay courts under Aleppo pines in a nine-hectare park by the sea
courts.blurb:
During the Cannes Film Festival, the biggest stars don't sleep in Cannes. They drive to the tip of Cap d'Antibes, to Hotel du Cap, which has been hiding famous guests since 1870. F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote it into Tender Is the Night, and its seawater pool cut into the rock is where the Riviera summer began.

The hotel sits in a nine-hectare park that runs down to the sea. Deep inside it, far from the cameras, are five clay courts under Aleppo pines, palms and olive trees. Between sets, the Mediterranean is only a short walk through the gardens. Red clay, green shade and the sound of the ball. On the most photographed coast in the world, this is the one place where nobody is watching you play.

courts.name: Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat, A Four Seasons Hotel
courts.setting: Clay courts in seven-hectare grounds at the tip of the cape
courts.blurb:
Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat sits at the tip of Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, its seven-hectare grounds meeting the Mediterranean. Clay-court tennis belongs to the same garden world as the hotel’s terraces and coastal paths.

Opened in January 1908, the hotel still carries its Belle Époque beginnings. Its original Rotunda was designed by Gustave Eiffel. The estate also includes Villa Rose-Pierre, with its own clay court. A garden match, a sea-facing pause, the Riviera unhurried.

courts.name: Château de la Messardière
courts.setting: Two sunken courts in twelve hectares of gardens above Saint-Tropez
courts.blurb:
Château de la Messardière rises in the hills above Saint-Tropez, surrounded by the vineyards of Ramatuelle. Two sunken tennis courts sit within twelve hectares of gardens and parasol pines, a quieter world above the coast.

The château began as a nineteenth-century wedding gift from cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d’Angeac to his daughter Louise and cavalry officer Henry Brisson de La Messardière. After Henry’s death, Louise turned it into a hotel, drawing Parisian aristocracy during the Roaring Twenties. A private love story became a Riviera address; tennis keeps its garden rhythm.
